chapter: Lee Collins and the riverboat Washington
title: Life aboard the Washington and the Red River route
summary: He describes the cooks, red and green lights in Monroe, the boat Washington and passing Angola.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Working the Streckfus riverboats with Fate Marable

blocks.x: He slept on the boat, huh? Yeah, he slept eight on the boat. They had two or three good cooks, catch that big old fish right out there, the red river and the river, you know, and everything.

They had one of them down on them. I used to draw my money going up the river and coming back and the captain's wife's daughter said, oh, Al don't know no better, you'll pay me again when I get you. It won't be better than the last twenty minutes. You see he had a brother who had a big old steam launch that cooled it, H.V. Cooler in Monroe, you know. And that's where the first time I saw red lights and green lights, that was out there before they got here in New Orleans. You understand what I mean? And to see a street was just like Ramport and Connell and they stuck together. And we used to go there and lay over and get there early and then he'd visit his brother and we'd go to Sturlton. That's seven miles, that's all the oil fields up there, you know. We'd run them excursions out there. What was the name of the boat?
What was the name of the river?
Washington. No wonder I'm next. I didn't know whether you were on the boat or the boat.

See, the Washington used to haul cotton. It'd run from here around Camp E, around Angola, branch off, or branch what deserted the Mississippi River, they called it the Old River. And it would go through the Old River, the Beth River, the Tennisaw River, used to cross it, isn't like crossing the street. It'd be a Red River and then when you're running out of the Red River, even to the Black River, and the Black River would run from there wherever it was until to Jonesville, and the Washington would take it home.
What was it like to go by Angola? Did you play any numbers for the press?

No, well they had high levels. You couldn't see too much. But I wasn't particular about it. You didn't want to go home to Angola. Yeah, certainly when we'd be coming back in the morning around four o'clock, we'd hear them coming in like that. We wouldn't, but other than that we wouldn't, we wouldn't, no, and we wouldn't go out of the place.
